seo.title: Karmic tail 15 8 20 compatibility: the Devil, Justice, Judgement
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 8 20 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, Justice in the middle, Judgement as the main task, read through Tolstoy's Resurrection.

title: Karmic tail 15-8-20 in compatibility: The Devil, Justice and Judgement
short: A hundred roubles in an envelope: in Tolstoy's Resurrection this sum opens an account between two people that neither money nor marriage can close. The couple's karmic tail 15-8-20 tells the same story. The couple enters the task through the Devil: an attraction that easily starts to name a price. It passes through the middle by way of Justice: an attempt to settle up and make amends. And its main task is Judgement: to stop keeping accounts and wake up to a life in which nobody pays with themselves.

sections.h2: A hundred roubles: where the story came from
paragraphs: In June 1887 the lawyer Anatoly Koni was a guest at Yasnaya Polyana and told Tolstoy a case from his years as a prosecutor in St Petersburg. A young man from high society had come to him asking to pass a letter to a prisoner, Rozalia Oni. Her story went like this. An orphan, the daughter of a tenant farmer, she grew up in the house of a rich St Petersburg lady; at sixteen she was seduced by a relative of her mistress, and when she became pregnant, the mistress turned her out. Rozalia gave the baby to a foundling home and slowly sank to the very bottom. One day, in a den near the Haymarket, she stole a hundred roubles from a drunken guest. She was tried before a jury, and among the jurors, by chance, sat the very man who had seduced her. He recognised her and decided to marry her.
Koni tried to talk him out of it and advised him to get to know his bride first. Lent put off the wedding, and at the end of Lent Rozalia died of typhus. That was where the real story ended.

Tolstoy asked Koni for the plot and for years called the project "the Koni story" in his diary. He wrote it on and off for ten years, finished it on 16 December 1899, and gave the fee to the resettlement of the Doukhobors in Canada. He called the novel Resurrection (Voskreseniye). Quotations below follow Louise Maude's translation of 1900; where the translation is ours, it is marked.

One detail changed sides on its way from life into the book. In Rozalia's case the hundred roubles are stolen money, the money she is tried for. In the novel the same sum ends up in another hand: it is the hundred-rouble note the seducer pushes on the girl as he leaves. The money she was tried for became the money with which he tried to close his account.

The novel's three acts follow the order of the tail. The Easter night and the envelope are the Devil. The jury room and the attempt to pay are Justice. Siberia, the refusal and the Gospel in the last chapter are Judgement. The novel is not a portrait of any particular couple, nor a script waiting for one: Tolstoy pushed everything to the limit. But the mechanism he took apart on an extreme case can be recognised, in a softer form, in ordinary married life.

sections.h2: The entry: the Devil, or love that names a price
paragraphs: Point M is the entry to the task: what the couple wants together, what it agrees on, which common language it speaks. It lies on the line of tasks, so the same desire that brought two people together can in time become resistance.

The Easter matins is the brightest scene in Resurrection. To Nekhlyudov it seems that everything in the church exists for Katyusha, "because she was the centre of all". Tolstoy calls that night the zenith of love, a moment when it is "unconscious, unreasoning, and with nothing sensual about it". A few hours later the hero is ruled by "the animal man, seeking only his own happiness", as Tolstoy calls him. And Nekhlyudov does what, as it seems to him, everyone does.

The most exact word about the Devil comes the next day. As he leaves, Nekhlyudov decides he must give her money, "not for her sake, not because she might need it, but because that is what is always done, and he would be thought dishonest if, having made use of her, he did not pay for it" (our translation; Maude softens the line). He pushes the envelope at her and runs to his room "as if he had burnt himself" (our translation). **Closeness converted into payment, and called honesty into the bargain**: that is this tail's entry in its extreme form.

Waite describes the Devil as the chain of material life and adds that the one exalted above the chained figures is not free either: he is "blind to the liberty of service". For Benebell Wen the Devil is above all a "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification". Tolstoy hears the same voice: "Take care I don't let the opportunity for your own happiness, your own enjoyment, slip by!" Wen and Tolstoy alike see here not a monster but ordinary human selfishness.

In an ordinary couple, 15 at the entry is not a drama of seduction. It is a common language in which closeness is easily translated into what was given and what was received. After a quarrel an expensive present turns up instead of a talk. In an argument someone says "I gave you everything". A decision rests on "that's how everyone lives". One partner wants the other to be theirs alone, and jealousy passes itself off as love. Among the tasks of a couple with this energy, Lisovskaya names attempts to hold on to the partner through closeness, money, status or a child, silence about one's own desires, and a union that drags both down. Her main thought about the fifteenth energy is short: **nobody belongs to anybody**.

The entry has its strength too. Fifteen gives a couple the courage to want and to speak openly about desire, to accept each other's dark sides and to forgive mistakes. The danger is not desire but the moment when "I want you" turns into "you owe me".

sections.h2: The middle: Justice, or the attempt to pay
paragraphs: Point N is the middle of the task. Lisovskaya gives it no meaning of its own; it completes the main task. We read it as the couple's path from the desire of M to the task of D: what the two do and what they go through.

Ten years later Nekhlyudov sits on a jury and recognises the defendant. In the jury room he thinks: "Yes, all that horrible business had not yet happened on that Easter eve!" The Easter night and the room where a verdict is reached stand in a single sentence: the tail's entry meets its middle.

Then Tolstoy shows how human judgement works. The jury finds Maslova guilty "without intent to rob" and forgets to add "without intent to take life". Tolstoy lists the reasons. This time the presiding judge forgot to suggest the wording. The colonel told the story of his brother-in-law's wife at great length. Nekhlyudov was too excited. One juror had left the room. And "chiefly because, being tired, and wishing to get away as soon as possible, all were ready to agree with the decision which would bring matters to an end soonest". An innocent woman is sent to four years of penal servitude. Nekhlyudov's first feeling is relief: "Siberia and penal servitude at once cut off every possibility of any kind of relations with her."

In a couple, a verdict like that is reached at half past one in the morning, when both are too tired to argue. The decision is taken not because it is right but because after it one can go to bed. Justice in its minus, for Lisovskaya, means both failing to notice that the partner is hurt and the habit of measuring everything by oneself.

Then comes the attempt to pay. In prison Nekhlyudov says he wants "to atone for my sin, not by mere words, but in deed. I have made up my mind to marry you." Katyusha answers: "You did not feel so then, but threw me 100 roubles. That's your price." And then: **"You've got pleasure out of me in this life, and want to save yourself through me in the life to come."** The whole tail is in one sentence: the Devil ("pleasure"), Judgement ("save yourself") and, between them, an account in which she twice becomes the means of payment.

Tolstoy himself stumbled at this step. On 5 January 1897 he wrote in his diary: "I began rereading Resurrection and, when I reached his decision to marry, threw it aside in disgust. It is all untrue, invented, weak" (our translation). To save the book he resolved "to describe his and her feelings and life by turns". A Justice that weighs only one pan stops being justice.

But the middle is not useless. Leaving the prison, Nekhlyudov understands: "If he had not tried to expiate his guilt he would never have found out how great his crime was. Nor was this all; she, too, would never have felt the whole horror of what had been done to her." **The attempt to pay shows the real size of the debt**, and shows that it cannot be closed with money or with marriage. The scales in the middle of the tail are there to see what happened, not to settle the account.

Wen has an exact pair of formulas for this card. Justice upright: "What is fair will feel fair." Reversed: "What is fair will not feel fair." Nekhlyudov's proposal is fair by the ledger, yet to Katyusha it sounds like a new price. Tolstoy names another trap of this card: until then Nekhlyudov "had played with a sensation of self-admiration, had admired his own remorse". The pleasure of being in the right is also a payment to oneself.

In a couple's life the middle 8 shows in small things. A tally runs in someone's head: who gave in how many times, who pulled whom out. An apology becomes a project: one partner is ready to do everything but never asks whether it is wanted. Help is later presented as a bill. After a quarrel someone says "we're quits". Among the tasks of the eight, Lisovskaya names owning one's guilt instead of blaming everyone; over-responsibility that turns into control and pressure; debts; forgiveness. In its plus the same card gives honest agreements, clear rules and "a cool head and a warm heart".

sections.h2: The main task: Judgement, or "Where is the use of our reckoning?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, its chief trials. It is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the two and what they have to learn.

Lisovskaya's key to the twentieth energy is kin and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. In its minus this is a union "for the sake of something", love hindered by age, status or tradition, a partner who decides nothing without the parents, and an inability to admit one's own mistake.

In Resurrection the family court speaks before any other. When he learns that Katyusha left to give birth and "had gone quite to the bad", Nekhlyudov hears from his aunts that "she had inherited her mother's depraved nature". Tolstoy adds: "he was pleased to hear this opinion of his aunts'. It seemed to acquit him." **The family's verdict suits whoever needs to be acquitted.** Next to it stands the difference in station that Katyusha throws in his face: "I am a convict and you a prince." And a marriage "for the sake of something": for the sake of his salvation.

The turn comes in Siberia. Waite's divinatory list for Judgement begins with the words "Change of position, renewal, outcome". Katyusha's sentence is commuted, and Nekhlyudov comes to tell her she may settle wherever she likes. She answers that she will follow the political prisoner Simonson. "No, Dmitri Ivanovitch, you must forgive me if I am not doing what you wish... You must live, too." She tries to thank him, he refuses her thanks, and she answers: **"Where is the use of our reckoning? God will make up our accounts."** At parting she says, as Tolstoy notes, not "Good-bye" but "Forgive me". In Russian both words, proshchaite and prostite, are imperatives of one verb, "to forgive", in its two aspects.

Before Siberia, Nekhlyudov wrote in his diary that Katyusha "does not wish to accept my sacrifice; she wishes to make a sacrifice herself. She has conquered, and so have I." And further: "she seems to be coming back to life".

The last chapter closes the books for good. At night in a hotel Nekhlyudov opens the Gospel an Englishman had given him and lands on Matthew 18. There is the parable of the hundred sheep, and then Peter's question: "How oft shall my brother offend me and I forgive him? Until seven times?" — and the answer: "until seventy times seven". The novel opens with these same verses; they are its epigraph. Then comes the parable of "a certain king which made a reckoning with his servants". The king forgives a servant a debt of ten thousand talents, and the servant goes out and takes by the throat a fellow-servant who owes him "a hundred pence". "And is this all?" Nekhlyudov exclaims aloud, and the inner voice answers: "Yes, it is all."

**The novel that began with a hundred roubles ends with a hundred pence**, a hundred denarii in the Russian text. Between them lies the whole course of the tail: from a price, through the account, to a judgement that stops counting. It becomes clear to Nekhlyudov that "we should forgive always an infinite number of times because there are no men who have not sinned themselves".

Waite writes that Judgement is a transformation in answer to a summons which "is heard and answered from within". Wen adds: "Events currently happening in the Seeker's life will be the catalyst to a personal awakening." For Nekhlyudov the catalyst was the "strange coincidence" in court which, in Tolstoy's words, "demanded from him the acknowledgment" of what he had done.

For the couple, the main task 20 is to own its part without putting the other on trial. To keep its own judgement apart from the family's verdict. Not to turn the union into a means of salvation. To let the other live their own life, as Katyusha let Nekhlyudov: "You must live, too." To forgive not from above, writing off a debt, but by ceasing to keep it. In its plus the twentieth energy gives a couple what Tolstoy's heroes so lacked: a union in which a difference in age, status or faith does not get in the way, mistakes are forgiven, and a partner is supported even when in the wrong.

sections.h2: A clue in the numbers: the Devil and Judgement on the scales
paragraphs: The strangest detail of this tail shows up in the arithmetic. 15 + 20 = 35, and 3 + 5 = 8. **Justice in the middle is the sum of the Devil and Judgement.** The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the middles of the two people's personal tails. And still the same sum comes out.
The couple's tail 15-8-20 is built from two combinations of personal tails:

ul: **6-20-14 and 9-15-6 — 79% of such couples.** Judgement stands in the middle of one person's personal tail, the Devil in the middle of the other's. 20 + 15 = 35, an eight. Both ends of the couple's tail are already in the personal charts, and their meeting gives the scales.
**6-17-11 and 9-18-9 — 21% of such couples.** The middles hold the Star and the Moon, hope and fog. 17 + 18 = 35, an eight again.

paragraphs: In both cases the entry 15 is made of one partner's Lovers (6) and the other's Hermit (9). The Lovers are not in the couple's tail, but in 79% of couples they appear in both personal tails: at the entry for one, at the end for the other. Like the Easter night Nekhlyudov remembers all his life: the love was there, but it enters the couple's shared story already as the Devil.

This is not a casting of roles. Whoever has 15 in their personal tail is not "the couple's Devil", and whoever has 20 is not its judge: a personal tail has its own points and its own meaning. In the novel both pans belong to both. Nekhlyudov carries both the "animal man" and the resurrection. Katyusha first defends herself with the same price, "my price is a ten-rouble note", and then decides her own fate and, in Nekhlyudov's words, is "coming back to life". The scales stand between two people, not in the hands of one of them.

sections.h2: The atmosphere: Death or the Emperor at the centre
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere: what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For the tail 15-8-20 the centre depends on which personal tails have met. In 79% of couples (6-20-14 and 9-15-6) it is 13, Death; in 21% (6-17-11 and 9-18-9) it is 4, the Emperor.

**Death between the Devil and Judgement.** In the real story Koni told, there is no resurrection: Rozalia died at the end of Lent, before the wedding. Life stopped at death, and Tolstoy called the book Resurrection. Waite writes that Death also has an entrance "while still in this life", as a change in the form of consciousness. Before leaving for Siberia, Nekhlyudov says the same in his own words in his diary: "Tomorrow a new life will begin. A final good-bye to the old!" In such a couple's atmosphere something is always ending. Lisovskaya sees in the plus of the thirteenth energy a couple that accepts the partner's past and moves on, takes changes in each other easily and helps the other out of destructive relationships. In the minus one forces the other to change and notices only the other's mistakes. The question of the atmosphere is whether endings become renewal or merely losses.

**The Emperor at the centre.** Where the centre is 4, the atmosphere is held by rules, order and someone's power to decide. In the novel this is the whole machinery of the state: the Senate, the petition to the Emperor, the paper with the pardon. In Waite's divinatory list the Emperor reversed reads "Benevolence, compassion, credit": mercy lives inside the same card as power. Lisovskaya describes, in the plus, passion, trust and strictness without fanaticism behind an outward reserve; in the minus, rigid rules, control and decisions made for everyone.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the World, the Empress, the Hanged Man
paragraphs: "The couple's values" in the compatibility matrix is the spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. For the tail 15-8-20 it is the World for 57.7% of couples, the Empress for 31% and the Hanged Man for 11.3%. Our reading: all three appear in the last part of Resurrection as three different answers to the question "what for".

ul: **The Empress — a home and the continuation of life.** In the general's house Nekhlyudov is shown the sleeping children and feels envious. An hour later, seeing Katyusha come in, he thinks: "I wish to live, I want a family, children, I want a human life."

**The Hanged Man — a sacrifice, but one's own.** Nekhlyudov realises that Katyusha may "not in the least require the sacrifice I imagined I was bringing her". In his diary he writes that she "does not wish to accept my sacrifice; she wishes to make a sacrifice herself". Wen links Justice reversed directly to the Hanged Man reversed, to "martyrdom": resentment at injustice easily turns into sacrifice for show.

**The World — a life in which nobody needs to be owned.** The last chapter goes beyond a single couple: Nekhlyudov thinks of a new order of life for everyone. Lisovskaya names in the World's plus full acceptance of the partner even in the minus and no pressure; in its minus, remaking the partner to suit oneself.

paragraphs: For a tail that begins with a price, the values sound like an answer: a home, not a deal; a sacrifice by one's own choice, not as payment; a world big enough for nobody to belong to anybody.

sections.h2: How the tail 15-8-20 is formed, and why it is not a personal programme
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is above 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends; it, too, is added up from the personal middles.

Example: the couple born 08.01.1976 and 14.05.1976. For the first person the day is 8, the month 1, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10, entry to the tail 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, middle 14 + 6 = 20. Personal tail: 6-20-14. For the second, the day is 14, the month 5, the year 5. Task 14 + 5 + 5 = 24 → 6, centre 14 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 30 → 3, entry 6 + 3 = 9, middle 6 + 9 = 15. Personal tail: 9-15-6.
Their couple's centre is 10 + 3 = 13, Death, and the couple's values are 21, the World. This is the most common combination of those described above.

In a personal matrix this triple never occurs. There the tail's entry M equals the sum of the main task D and the centre. With D = 20, any such sum lies between 23 and 42 and reduces to 12 at most, so fifteen at the entry is impossible with any centre. If 15, 8 and 20 stand on a chart, it is a couple's chart.

The tail 15-8-20 is rare: it occurs in about one couple in 1,123 (0.089%) and ranks 83rd of the 97 couple tails. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: the Devil, Justice and Judgement meet on a couple's tail only in this order.

Resurrection has a judge, Matvei Nikitich, who likes to tell fortunes by numbers. Walking into the courtroom, he makes a guess about his new regimen: if the number of steps to his chair divides by three, the regimen will work. There are twenty-six steps, so he squeezes in a little extra one to make twenty-seven. At the decisive moment he adds up the figures of a number on a paper: if the sum divides by three, he will back the presiding judge. It does not divide, yet "his kindness made him agree all the same". The first number of a couple's tail also always divides by three, here it is 15, but that is a property of addition, not an omen. The tail's numbers do not tell the outcome. As in the novel, people decide.

sections.h2: Living the tail 15-8-20 at its strongest
paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is a couple whose desire is honest, whose agreements are clear, and whose past has been lived through rather than presented as a bill. Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fifteenth energy not to buy love with presents, and to admit their secret desires and talk about them. The novel itself suggests the rest.

ul: **Noticing the moment when a present, a favour or "after all I did for you" starts replacing a conversation.** That is the Devil's entry: desire being converted into a price.
**Not making important decisions "just to get it over with".** That is how Tolstoy's jury sent an innocent woman to penal servitude.
**Putting things right by asking what the other needs, not by assigning them one's own atonement.** Nekhlyudov proposes marriage and is told that he wants to save himself through her.
**Keeping one's own judgement apart from the family's.** The aunts' verdict suited, above all, the one who wanted to be acquitted.

**Starting with oneself.** Nekhlyudov writes in his diary: "If only we could manage to see the beam in our own eye in time, how kind we should be." It is the novel's second epigraph, retold in his own words.
**Forgiving means ceasing to keep the account,** not pretending that nothing happened.

paragraphs: Tolstoy did not promise his hero a happy ending. The last sentence of the novel reads: "How this new period of his life will end time alone will prove." The tail 15-8-20 promises nothing either and passes no sentence. It shows where an account begins between two people and where they can stop keeping it.

ul: **15 · The Devil — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together and which language it speaks: strong attraction, a wish to possess, and a habit of measuring closeness by what has been given and received.
**8 · Justice — middle of the task.** How the couple walks the path: weighing who owes whom, trying to put things right by deeds and to settle matters by the rules.

**20 · Judgement — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to own its part without looking for someone to blame, to keep its own judgement apart from the family's, and to forgive so that each can live their own life.

intro: People also look up "15 8 20" as a programme in the destiny matrix. In a personal chart, by our method, this tail does not occur: it belongs to couples. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the three numbers on a couple's tail its karmic programme. This is neither a forecast nor a verdict: the numbers show which story comes most easily to the couple and where it turns.

faq.q: What does 15-8-20 mean in a couple's destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the couple's karmic tail: the Devil at the entry to the task, Justice in the middle, Judgement as the main task. The story of the tail runs from closeness that starts being measured by price, through an attempt to settle up, to the ability to own one's part and forgive.

faq.q: Does 15-8-20 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the tail's entry equals the sum of the main task and the centre, and with a main task of 20 the entry cannot be fifteen. The triple 15-8-20 occurs only in a couple's matrix.

Lisovskaya calls the three numbers on a couple's tail its karmic programme. It is the same M–N–D triple, not a separate calculation: the programme describes the couple's tasks, not a fate assigned to it.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail is read mostly through its difficulties because it is about tasks, not about a verdict. In the plus the same cards give the courage to talk about desire, honest agreements and the ability to forgive.

faq.q: Which partner is the Devil and which is the judge?
faq.a: Neither. The numbers of a couple's tail belong to the couple as a whole. Even if one partner has 15 in their personal tail and the other has 20, these are not the roles of culprit and judge but two pans of the same scales.

captions.N: To try to settle up and make amends in deed
captions.D: To own your part, forgive and stop keeping score

unit.meaning: Your task is to stop keeping accounts: don't swap a talk for a present, and don't turn forgiveness into payment.
